## What I was responsible for

- **Partnership.** I worked with a partner all semester to build up our understanding of the electronics, from breadboarding to a finished board, and to apply systems concepts to real devices that could gather data.
- **PCB.** I assembled the PCB containing the MCP6002 op-amp that conditions the sensor signals and returns their output voltages.
- **Soldering and testing.** I soldered each circuit and tested it with an oscilloscope and a DMM to verify signal integrity before deployment.
- **Analysis.** I modeled and analyzed the output voltages in LabVIEW to interpret the sensor readings.

## Results

We deployed the ROV at a local lake. Its depth controller used proportional (Kp) control, and the graph below shows the logged depth against the commanded depth over about four minutes of the run.

```{=html}
<div class="pj-row" style="max-width:720px;margin-left:auto;margin-right:auto">
  <figure><img src="../images/web/rov_depth.jpg" alt="ROV depth vs desired depth during the lake deployment"><figcaption>Measured depth (blue) vs. desired depth (red) during the lake deployment. The ROV was commanded between about 0.2 m and 1.0 m.</figcaption></figure>
</div>
```

The ROV followed each depth command. It rose to 1.0 m and held it with small oscillations, then dropped back to about 0.2 m, and it repeated this on several cycles.

## What I learned

The project let us take systems-engineering ideas out of the textbook and use them on hardware we built ourselves: sensors, signal conditioning and data analysis, working together as a pair. By the end I was comfortable designing, soldering, testing and debugging the electronics that turn a physical measurement into usable data.

## Why a cost-effective ROV

Underwater ROVs are a cost-effective way to gather environmental data in aquatic settings. The goal was a vehicle robust enough for real lake deployment while still buildable within the limits of a course project.
